stem_fields.name: Lactic acid
stem_fields.note: A carboxylate shares its charge between two oxygens; an alkoxide keeps it on one.

sites.what: alkyl C–H, as in an alkane

stem_fields.name: Propargyl alcohol
stem_fields.note: Oxygen carries a negative charge far better than carbon, even an sp carbon.

stem_fields.name: Propargylamine
stem_fields.note: Here the C–H wins: an acetylide is more stable than an amide anion R–NH⁻. That is why NaNH₂ deprotonates terminal alkynes.

stem_fields.name: Ethanolamine
stem_fields.note: Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen. The amine is the basic site of this molecule, not the acidic one.

stem_fields.name: Ethanolammonium
stem_fields.note: Once the amine is protonated, its N–H is the acidic proton: losing it gives a neutral amine, not an anion.

stem_fields.name: 2-Mercaptoethanol
stem_fields.note: The S–H bond is weaker than O–H and the large sulfur atom spreads the charge, so a thiol is about a million times more acidic than an alcohol.

stem_fields.name: 4-Hydroxybenzyl alcohol
stem_fields.note: The phenoxide charge is delocalised into the ring. The CH₂ cuts the alkoxide off from it.

sites.what: alcohol O–H, as in benzyl alcohol

stem_fields.name: 4-Hydroxybenzoic acid
stem_fields.note: Both O–H are acidic, but the carboxylate shares its charge between two equivalent oxygens.

stem_fields.name: 4-Hydroxyacetophenone
stem_fields.note: The para acetyl group takes the phenoxide charge onto its oxygen, so this phenol is stronger than phenol itself (9.95).

stem_fields.name: Acetamide
stem_fields.note: The N–H anion is shared between N and O. The α C–H of an amide is the least acidic of all carbonyl α-protons.

stem_fields.name: 4-Aminophenol
stem_fields.note: Both anions are delocalised into the ring, so electronegativity decides: O beats N.

stem_fields.name: Acetylacetone
stem_fields.note: The CH₂ between two carbonyls gives an enolate shared by both oxygens.

sites.what: C–H next to one C=O, as in acetone

stem_fields.name: Ethyl acetoacetate
stem_fields.note: The doubly activated CH₂ is the carbon alkylated in the acetoacetic ester synthesis.

sites.what: C–H between the ketone and the ester
C–H next to the ketone only, as in acetone

stem_fields.name: 1,3-Cyclohexanedione
stem_fields.note: Two carbonyls bring this C–H down to the acidity of acetic acid.

sites.what: C–H next to one C=O, as in acetone
C–H next to no C=O, as in an alkane

stem_fields.name: Phenylacetone
stem_fields.note: Both are α to the ketone, but the benzylic enolate is also conjugated with the ring.

sites.what: benzylic C–H next to the C=O
methyl C–H next to the C=O, as in acetone

stem_fields.name: Methyl levulinate
stem_fields.note: A ketone is more acidic at its α-carbon than an ester: the ester's OR group already donates into its C=O.

sites.what: C–H next to the ketone, as in acetone
C–H next to the ester, as in ethyl acetate

stem_fields.name: Cyclopentadiene
stem_fields.note: Removing a CH₂ proton gives the cyclopentadienyl anion, which is aromatic (6 π electrons).

stem_fields.name: p-Nitrotoluene
stem_fields.note: The nitro group takes the benzylic charge by resonance. Toluene itself is 43 in DMSO.

stem_fields.name: Phenylacetylene
stem_fields.note: More s character holds the anion's lone pair closer to the nucleus: sp beats sp².

stem_fields.name: Glycine, fully protonated
stem_fields.note: The nearby NH₃⁺ makes this CO₂H much stronger than acetic acid (4.76). At pH 7 glycine is a zwitterion.

stem_fields.name: Glutamic acid, fully protonated
stem_fields.note: Both are carboxylic acids, but the α one sits next to the positive NH₃⁺, which stabilises its carboxylate.

stem_fields.name: Histidine, fully protonated
stem_fields.note: Imidazolium (6.0) is the group that lets histidine buffer near pH 7 in proteins.

stem_fields.name: Tyrosine, fully protonated
stem_fields.note: Order of loss: CO₂H, then NH₃⁺, then the phenol.

stem_fields.name: Cysteine, fully protonated
stem_fields.note: Order of loss: CO₂H, then the thiol, then NH₃⁺.

stem_fields.name: Salicylic acid
stem_fields.note: An H-bond from the OH holds the carboxylate, so this is a strong benzoic acid. The same H-bond makes the phenol unusually weak.

stem_fields.name: Aspirin
stem_fields.note: Its only acidic group in water is the carboxylic acid.

sites.what: acetyl C–H, as in ethyl acetate

stem_fields.name: Paracetamol
stem_fields.note: Paracetamol is a phenol. The amide N–H is far weaker.

stem_fields.name: Sulfanilamide
stem_fields.note: The sulfonyl group spreads the N⁻ charge onto two oxygens. In water the sulfonamide pKa is about 10.

stem_fields.name: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C)
stem_fields.note: The C3 anion is a vinylogous carboxylate: its charge reaches the lactone C=O through the C=C.

stem_fields.name: Propene
stem_fields.note: A radical chain: Br· adds first, to CH₂, giving the more stable secondary radical; the H comes last.

stem_fields.name: 2-Methylbutane
stem_fields.ask: Which C–H is brominated?
stem_fields.note: Bromination is very selective: the tertiary radical forms fastest.

stem_fields.name: Propylbenzene
stem_fields.ask: Which C–H is brominated?
stem_fields.note: The benzylic radical is stabilised by the ring.

stem_fields.name: 4-Methylquinoline (lepidine)
stem_fields.ask: Where does the t-Bu radical attack?
stem_fields.note: A Minisci reaction: acid protonates the quinoline, which leaves C2 and C4 electron-poor, and the nucleophilic t-Bu radical (from pivalic acid) attacks there. C4 already carries the methyl.

stem_signature: site|4-methylquinoline (lepidine)|t-buco2h, agno3, (nh4)2s2o8, h2so4|where does the t-bu radical attack?

stem_fields.name: 2-Methylquinoline (quinaldine)
stem_fields.ask: Where does the t-Bu radical attack?
stem_fields.note: With C2 blocked, the nucleophilic radical takes the other electron-poor position of the quinolinium ion, C4.

stem_signature: site|2-methylquinoline (quinaldine)|t-buco2h, agno3, (nh4)2s2o8, h2so4|where does the t-bu radical attack?

stem_fields.name: N-Methylpyrrole
stem_fields.ask: Where does the •CF₃ radical attack?
stem_fields.note: •CF₃ is an electrophilic radical, so it behaves like an electrophile: it attacks the electron-rich C2 of the pyrrole.

stem_signature: site|n-methylpyrrole|cf3so2na, t-buooh (•cf3)|where does the •cf3 radical attack?

stem_fields.name: Methyl acrylate
stem_fields.ask: Where does the cyclohexyl radical add?
stem_fields.note: Giese addition: the nucleophilic radical adds to the unhindered β-carbon, where the LUMO is largest, and leaves a radical stabilised by the ester.

stem_signature: site|methyl acrylate|cyclohexyl radical (c-hexi, bu3snh, aibn)|where does the cyclohexyl radical add?

stem_fields.name: Tetrahydrofuran
stem_fields.ask: Which C–H does Cl• abstract?
stem_fields.note: Polarity matching in hydrogen-atom transfer: the electrophilic Cl• abstracts the hydridic C–H next to oxygen, and the nucleophilic α-oxy radical it leaves is then coupled by nickel.

stem_signature: site|tetrahydrofuran|cl• (photoredox, ni–cl)|which c–h does cl• abstract?

stem_fields.name: Cyclopentanone
stem_fields.ask: Which C–H does decatungstate abstract?
stem_fields.note: The α-C–H bonds next to the carbonyl are electron-poor, so the electrophilic excited decatungstate avoids them and abstracts a β-hydrogen, although the α radical would be the more stable one.

stem_signature: site|cyclopentanone|tbadt (decatungstate), hν|which c–h does decatungstate abstract?

stem_fields.name: tert-Butyl radical
stem_fields.note: Three alkyl groups donate into the singly occupied orbital (SOMO) by hyperconjugation and raise it: tertiary alkyl radicals are strongly nucleophilic and add fast to acrylates (Giese reaction). The bulk does not slow them as it would an anion, because the transition state is early, with a long forming bond (2.55 Å for t-Bu• adding to methyl vinyl ketone).
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Isopropyl radical
stem_fields.note: Secondary alkyl radicals are nucleophilic: two alkyl groups raise the SOMO. Ethyl and isopropyl radicals made from ethane and propane add to Michael acceptors.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Methyl radical
stem_fields.note: Ambiphilic: the high-energy methyl radical barely discriminates between electron-rich and electron-poor alkenes. Under mild conditions it reacts as a nucleophile, adding to Michael acceptors and to azodicarboxylates.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Cyanomethyl radical
stem_fields.note: One electron-withdrawing group is enough to make a primary radical electrophilic: the nitrile's π* accepts density from the SOMO and lowers it. Cyanoalkyl radicals add to electron-rich enamines.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: (Ethoxycarbonyl)methyl radical
stem_fields.note: A primary radical with one ester is electrophilic: α-carbonyl radicals add to enamines and enol ethers.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: 2-(Methoxycarbonyl)prop-2-yl radical
stem_fields.note: A tertiary radical with a single ester is still nucleophilic: it is the growing chain end when methyl methacrylate polymerises, adding to the electron-poor monomer. Secondary and tertiary radicals need two electron-withdrawing groups to turn electrophilic.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Diethyl malonyl radical
stem_fields.note: Two esters lower the SOMO enough to make even a secondary radical electrophilic: malonyl radicals add to indoles and other electron-rich arenes.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Hydroxymethyl radical
stem_fields.note: The oxygen lone pair donates into the SOMO (n → p) and raises it: α-oxy radicals are strongly nucleophilic, even though oxygen is electronegative.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Tetrahydrofuran-2-yl radical
stem_fields.note: An α-oxy radical, among the most nucleophilic radicals known. Cl• or decatungstate hydrogen-atom transfer makes it from THF, and it adds to electron-poor alkenes or to nickel.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: N-Boc-pyrrolidin-2-yl radical
stem_fields.note: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so α-amino radicals are even more nucleophilic, and they stay so with a Boc group on nitrogen. They add to protonated heteroarenes (Minisci reactions) and are captured by nickel.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: (Methylthio)methyl radical
stem_fields.note: α-Sulfur radicals, like α-F, α-Cl, α-Br and α-I radicals, are moderately nucleophilic: the lone pair donates by π overlap. Made by metal-hydride HAT from vinyl sulfides, they add to acrylamides.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: (Trimethylsilyl)methyl radical
stem_fields.note: A primary α-silyl radical is electrophilic: the SOMO gives density to silicon's low-lying acceptor orbitals, which lowers it. With two more alkyl groups (a tertiary α-silyl radical) it is nucleophilic again.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: 2-(Dimethylphenylsilyl)prop-2-yl radical
stem_fields.note: A tertiary α-silyl radical is nucleophilic: it adds to methyl acrylate (Giese). The two alkyl groups outweigh silicon's acceptor effect, which wins only in primary and secondary α-silyl radicals.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Trifluoromethyl radical
stem_fields.note: Mostly electrophilic: three electronegative fluorines outweigh their π donation, and •CF₃ adds to electron-rich arenes and alkenes. It is ambiphilic, though, and also adds to some electron-poor heteroarenes and alkenes.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Difluoromethyl radical
stem_fields.note: Unlike •CF₃, •CF₂H reacts as a nucleophile with heteroarenes: it attacks protonated, electron-poor positions as alkyl radicals do in Minisci reactions.

stem_fields.name: Phenyl radical
stem_fields.note: A σ radical: the SOMO is an sp² orbital in the ring plane, at right angles to the π system, so ring substituents barely change it. Its s character makes it electrophilic, and its high energy makes it ambiphilic: aryl radicals add to electron-rich and electron-poor arenes alike.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: 2-Methylprop-1-enyl radical
stem_fields.note: Vinyl radicals are σ radicals with more s character than alkyl radicals: they are electrophilic and usually add to electron-rich or plain alkenes, which is why vinyl radical cyclisations onto unactivated alkenes work.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Phenylethynyl radical
stem_fields.note: Alkynyl radicals have the most s character of all and are electrophilic: in a competition, phenylethynyl radicals attack the more electron-rich of two arenes.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Acetyl radical
stem_fields.note: The oxygen lone pair is held in line with the SOMO, so acyl radicals are exceptionally nucleophilic: an umpolung of the electrophilic carbonyl carbon. They add to acrylonitriles and vinyl sulfones, giving ketones.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: tert-Butoxyl radical
stem_fields.note: Oxygen is far more electronegative than carbon (3.44 against 2.55), so oxyl radicals are strongly electrophilic. They seldom add to π bonds; they abstract hydridic H atoms (HAT) or fragment (β-scission).
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Piperidin-1-yl (aminyl) radical
stem_fields.note: N is more electronegative than C (3.04): aminyl radicals are electrophilic and aminate electron-rich arenes. Protonated, as aminium radical cations, they are more electrophilic still.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Piperidinium radical cation
stem_fields.note: Aminium radical cations are among the most electrophilic radicals: they add to electron-rich arenes and abstract hydridic C–H bonds next to O and N.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: N-Methylacetamidyl radical
stem_fields.note: Amidyl radicals are electrophilic N radicals: they add to electron-rich π systems and abstract δ-C–H bonds (1,5-HAT), as in Hofmann–Löffler-type remote functionalisation.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Butanethiyl radical
stem_fields.note: Sulfur is barely more electronegative than carbon (2.58 against 2.55), yet thiyl radicals are electrophilic: the thiol–ene reaction is fastest with electron-rich alkenes such as vinyl ethers and norbornene.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Bromine atom
stem_fields.note: Halogen atoms are strongly electrophilic: Br• adds to electron-rich alkenes (radical HBr addition) and picks out hydridic C–H bonds.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Chlorine atom
stem_fields.note: Cl• is one of the most electrophilic radicals: it abstracts the hydridic C–H next to the oxygen of THF, and nickel then couples the α-oxy radical.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Tris(trimethylsilyl)silyl radical
stem_fields.note: Silicon is less electronegative than carbon, so silyl radicals are nucleophilic: (TMS)₃Si• adds to methyl acrylate but not to 1-hexene or styrene, and abstracts halogen atoms fast.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: NHC–boryl radical
stem_fields.note: Boron is less electronegative than carbon (2.04): ligated boryl radicals are nucleophilic. An NHC–BH₂• radical added to methyl acrylate at least 380 times faster than to ethyl vinyl ether.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Diethoxyphosphoryl radical
stem_fields.note: Phosphonyl radicals, which carry a P=O, are electrophilic: they add to unactivated alkenes and enol ethers, although phosphorus is less electronegative than carbon.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: NHC–boryl radical
stem_fields.note: At least 380 times faster to the acrylate: a nucleophilic radical wants an electron-poor partner.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: tert-Butyl radical
stem_fields.note: The nucleophilic t-Bu• radical adds to the electron-poor alkene (a Giese addition); the electron-rich enol ether is a poor match.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Diethyl malonyl radical
stem_fields.note: Two esters make the malonyl radical electrophilic, so it adds to the electron-rich enol ether.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Tetrahydrofuran-2-yl radical
stem_fields.note: The α-oxy radical is strongly nucleophilic and adds to the acrylate; 1-hexene offers no polar help.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Butanethiyl radical
stem_fields.note: Thiyl radicals are electrophilic: in thiol–ene chemistry vinyl ethers react far faster than acrylates, which tend to polymerise instead.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Trifluoromethyl radical
stem_fields.note: •CF₃ is electrophilic and attacks the electron-rich pyrrole, at C2, like an electrophile would.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Acetyl radical
stem_fields.note: Acyl radicals are nucleophilic and add to electron-poor alkenes, giving ketones.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Tris(trimethylsilyl)silyl radical
stem_fields.note: The nucleophilic silyl radical adds to methyl acrylate; with 1-hexene or styrene no reaction was seen.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Piperidinium radical cation
stem_fields.note: The electrophilic aminium radical cation aminates electron-rich arenes such as anisole.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Cyanomethyl radical
stem_fields.note: One nitrile makes the primary radical electrophilic, so it prefers the electron-rich enol ether.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Bromine atom
stem_fields.note: Br• is electrophilic and adds to the electron-richer alkene.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: N-Boc-pyrrolidin-2-yl radical
stem_fields.note: The nucleophilic α-amino radical adds to the protonated, electron-poor heteroarene: a Minisci reaction.
src: Parsaee et al., Nat. Rev. Chem. 2021

stem_fields.name: Acetone enolate
stem_fields.note: Alkyl halides react at carbon. SN2 has a high intrinsic barrier, so the more stable product wins: C-alkylation keeps the strong C=O bond, O-alkylation would give a much less stable enol ether.

stem_fields.name: Acetone enolate
stem_fields.note: Silicon forms a very strong bond to oxygen, so silyl chlorides trap enolates on O: this is how silyl enol ethers are made.

stem_fields.name: 1-Pyrrolidinocyclohexene
stem_fields.note: Stork enamine reaction: attack at nitrogen is reversible, attack at the β-carbon gives a stable C–C bond. Mayr's N = 14.91 for this enamine describes the carbon.

stem_fields.name: Indole
stem_fields.note: At C3 the nitrogen stabilises the cation and the benzene ring stays intact.

stem_fields.name: Pyrrole
stem_fields.note: Attack at C2 gives a cation shared over three atoms, including N; attack at C3 shares it over only two.

stem_fields.name: Thiocyanate
stem_fields.note: Sulfur attacks faster (N = 17.9 for S, about 12 for N in MeCN). The more stable isothiocyanates, from N-attack, form only when the thiocyanate can come off and add again (thermodynamic control).

stem_fields.name: Cyanide
stem_fields.note: Nitriles form. Isocyanides appear only with diffusion-controlled carbocations or with silver cyanide, where Ag⁺ blocks the carbon end.

stem_fields.name: Phenoxide
stem_fields.note: Williamson ether synthesis: O-alkylation leaves the ring aromatic; attack by a ring carbon would first break the aromaticity.

stem_fields.name: Aniline
stem_fields.note: The amine nitrogen is the nucleophile towards acylating agents; the ring only reacts with strong electrophiles such as Br₂.

stem_fields.name: 4-Aminophenol
stem_fields.note: This is how paracetamol is made: the amine is the better nucleophile, so acetylation stops at the amide.

stem_fields.name: Ethanolamine
stem_fields.note: Amines are much better nucleophiles than alcohols (Mayr N = 14.1 for ethanolamine's nitrogen in MeCN, against about 7 for an alcohol).

stem_fields.name: L-Cysteinate
stem_fields.note: Thiolates are far more nucleophilic than amines: N = 23.4 for cysteine's thiolate against 13.5 for glycinate's amine, both in water.

stem_fields.name: Allyltrimethylsilane
stem_fields.note: Attack at the far end puts the positive charge β to silicon, where the C–Si bond stabilises it; then the silyl group leaves.

stem_fields.name: 1-(Trimethylsiloxy)cyclohexene
stem_fields.note: Mukaiyama aldol reaction: the silyl enol ether attacks with its α-carbon.

stem_fields.name: Ethyl vinyl ether
stem_fields.note: Attack at the terminal CH₂ leaves the positive charge next to oxygen, which stabilises it (an oxocarbenium ion).

stem_fields.name: DMAP
stem_fields.note: The NMe₂ lone pair is delocalised into the ring and onto the ring nitrogen, which attacks and forms the N-acetylpyridinium ion.

stem_fields.name: Imidazole
stem_fields.note: The lone pair of the N–H nitrogen is part of the aromatic sextet; the other nitrogen's lone pair is free.

stem_fields.name: DBU
stem_fields.note: Amidines react at the sp² nitrogen: the cation formed is shared by both nitrogens.

stem_fields.name: Hydroxylamine
stem_fields.note: Nitrogen attacks, so carbonyl compounds give oximes.

stem_fields.name: Ethyl acetoacetate dianion
stem_fields.note: The second proton comes off the less acidic CH₃. That carbanion is the more basic, less stabilised one, so it reacts first (Weiler alkylation).

stem_fields.name: 2-Pyridone anion
stem_fields.note: Alkali salts give mainly N-methyl-2-pyridone, which keeps a strong C=O bond; silver salts give the O-alkylated 2-alkoxypyridine.

stem_fields.name: Cyclohexenone
stem_fields.note: Cuprates add 1,4 (conjugate addition).

stem_fields.name: Cyclohexenone
stem_fields.note: Organolithiums add fast and irreversibly to the carbonyl carbon (1,2-addition).

stem_fields.name: Methyl vinyl ketone
stem_fields.note: Stabilised enolates add 1,4 (Michael addition): addition to the C=O is reversible, the 1,4-adduct is not.

stem_fields.name: Ethyl acrylate
stem_fields.note: Aza-Michael addition at room temperature; aminolysis of the ester is much slower.

stem_fields.name: Methyl 4-formylbenzoate
stem_fields.note: Aldehydes are much more electrophilic than esters, whose C=O is stabilised by the OMe lone pair.

stem_fields.name: Methyl levulinate
stem_fields.note: NaBH₄ reduces ketones but esters only very slowly.

stem_fields.name: Methyl 4-(chlorocarbonyl)benzoate
stem_fields.note: Acid chlorides are the most reactive acyl derivatives: Cl donates little to the C=O and leaves easily.

stem_fields.name: Chloroacetyl chloride
stem_fields.note: Addition to the acyl chloride C=O is far faster than SN2 at CH₂Cl, so chloroacetamides form.

stem_fields.name: Phenacyl bromide
stem_fields.note: Amines add to ketones reversibly; SN2 next to a C=O is unusually fast, so the α-amino ketone forms.

stem_fields.name: Acetic formic anhydride
stem_fields.note: Formylation, not acetylation: the formyl carbon has no methyl group to donate electrons or block the approach.

stem_fields.name: Phenyl isocyanate
stem_fields.note: Amines add to the central carbon, giving ureas.

stem_fields.name: Ethyl 4-(ethylsulfanyl)-4-oxobutanoate
stem_fields.note: Thioesters are activated acyl groups: sulfur donates less to the C=O than oxygen and thiolate leaves easily. Nature uses them in acetyl-CoA, and chemists in native chemical ligation.

stem_fields.name: 4-Bromobenzyl bromide
stem_fields.note: SN2 is impossible at an sp² aryl carbon; at a benzylic carbon it is fast.

stem_fields.name: Butane-1,3-diyl dimesylate
stem_fields.note: SN2 is much faster at a primary carbon than at a secondary one.

stem_fields.name: 1-Fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene (Sanger's reagent)
stem_fields.note: SNAr: the nitro groups ortho and para to C1 hold the negative charge of the Meisenheimer complex, then fluoride leaves.

stem_fields.name: 4-Benzylidene-2,6-di-tert-butylcyclohexa-2,5-dienone
stem_fields.note: Attack at the exocyclic carbon turns the quinone methide into an aromatic phenolate.

stem_fields.name: Epichlorohydrin
stem_fields.note: Most nucleophiles open the strained epoxide at its less hindered carbon; the alkoxide formed then displaces chloride and closes a new epoxide.

stem_fields.name: Anisole
stem_fields.note: OMe donates into the ring, so ortho and para attack give a cation stabilised on oxygen. Para wins: it is less crowded.

stem_fields.name: Nitrobenzene
stem_fields.note: Ortho and para attack would put the positive charge next to the electron-poor nitro group; meta attack avoids that.

stem_fields.name: Benzaldehyde
stem_fields.note: Like NO₂, the CHO group withdraws electrons and directs meta.

stem_fields.name: Acetanilide
stem_fields.note: The amide nitrogen donates into the ring; the bulky NHAc group shields the ortho positions.

stem_fields.name: tert-Butylbenzene
stem_fields.note: Alkyl groups direct ortho and para; the bulky tert-butyl group blocks ortho.

stem_fields.name: Chlorobenzene
stem_fields.note: Halogens slow the reaction down but direct ortho and para: their lone pairs stabilise the cations formed there.

stem_fields.name: Toluene
stem_fields.note: Friedel–Crafts acylation is almost entirely para: the acylium–AlCl₄⁻ electrophile is bulky.

stem_fields.name: 4-Methylanisole
stem_fields.note: When two groups compete, the stronger donor decides: OMe beats CH₃.

stem_fields.name: 4-Nitrotoluene
stem_fields.note: Both groups agree: CH₃ directs ortho to itself and NO₂ directs meta to itself, which is the same carbon.

stem_fields.name: Pyrrole
stem_fields.note: Attack at C2 gives a cation shared over three atoms, including N; attack at C3 shares it over only two.

stem_fields.name: Indole
stem_fields.note: At C3 the nitrogen stabilises the cation without disrupting the benzene ring.

stem_fields.name: Furan
stem_fields.note: As with pyrrole: the cation from C2 attack is shared over three atoms.

stem_fields.name: Thiophene
stem_fields.note: As with furan and pyrrole, attack at C2 gives a cation shared over three atoms, one of them sulfur.
